metadata.title: Restart Required.
metadata.subtitle: The Plugin Settings Pattern
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you flip a setting in a Claude Code plugin's settings file, does it take effect right away? Take apart the pattern — one dot-local file, YAML frontmatter plus markdown body, three readers, per-project scope — and name the design trade-off: Anthropic optimized for project-scoped, git-safe configuration at the cost of a live reload and any cross-project carryover. Lands the carry-out that the file works per-project, not globally, and needs a restart before any change takes hold.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. Someone flipped a plugin's enabled flag in its settings file, saved, and expected the change to take. It didn't — Claude Code has to restart before any of it counts. So the real question isn't whether the toggle works. It's when.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. The pattern lives in exactly one file: dot-claude slash plugin-name dot local dot md, sitting in the project root. Two parts to it — YAML frontmatter for structured settings on top, a markdown body for prompts and instructions below. Three things read it: bash hooks, command files, and agent instructions, all pointed at the same file. It's per-project, it's user-managed, and it never gets committed to git. That last piece is the tell — Anthropic optimized for a config that stays local to the developer's machine, not one that ships with the plugin.

Four things have to be right for the pattern to actually work. One: design the schema first — what fields, what types — before any hook goes near it. Two: decide sensible defaults for when the file doesn't exist, because most users never create it. Three: hooks should quick-exit — check the file exists, check it's enabled, otherwise get out of the way. That's the difference between a plugin that fails open and a plugin that stalls the terminal. And four: every project needs its own gitignore entry for the file, and that step is manual — nothing auto-adds it. Skip any one of the four and the pattern starts leaking: schema drift, silent failures, hooks that hang, or private settings ending up in the repo.

beats.narration_text: One gap worth naming, because it's a design choice and not an oversight. A setting you configure in one project doesn't carry over to any other project — there's no plugin-wide switch, no user-global fallback. Every project keeps its own file, its own flags, its own restart. This works if you value strict project isolation — no plugin can change how it behaves in a repo you haven't opened. It fails if you value a single knob you set once. Anthropic picked isolation.

So here's the carry-out. A plugin's settings file works per project, not globally, and no change takes effect until Claude Code restarts. Set it, save it, restart it — that's the whole contract, and there isn't a shorter version.

props.quote: A plugin's settings file is per-project and needs a restart. Set it, save it, restart it — that's the whole contract.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no CLI, no plugin — that has the model draft the dot-local file itself for a plugin you're building: an enabled flag, a validation level, a max-retries count, plus the quick-exit hook that reads it and the gitignore line that keeps it out of the repo. Go deeper: could the same pattern support a user-global override — a single fallback file that per-project settings extend — without breaking the project-isolation guarantee? Draft the schema that would let both live at once.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm building a Claude Code plugin and I want to add per-project configuration using the .local.md pattern — a file at .claude/[plugin-name].local.md in the project root, with YAML frontmatter for settings and a markdown body for prompts. Please produce four things: (1) a sample .local.md file with three settings — an `enabled` boolean flag, a `validation_level` enum (`off` | `warn` | `strict`), and a `max_retries` integer — including sensible defaults inline and a short markdown body explaining each field; (2) a bash hook that reads the file, quick-exits if the file is missing or `enabled` is false, and otherwise reads `validation_level` and `max_retries`; (3) the exact .gitignore line to keep this file out of the repo; and (4) a two-line note on why the file has to be per-project and why a restart is required after editing it. Fail-open behavior throughout — a missing file is not an error.
